title: The adjoint-action kernel is the scheme-theoretic centre
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and let $G$ be a split reductive $A$-group scheme with split maximal torus $T=D_A(M)$, in the sense of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization] after forgetting the pinning. The scheme-theoretic centre $Z(G)$ is the subgroup functor of elements whose conjugation action on $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is the identity after every commutative algebra extension. Consequently, its intersection with $T$ is the subgroup functor of torus elements whose restricted conjugation action on $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is the identity. These kernel identifications are functorial under every base change $A\to B$, including nonreduced and disconnected base rings.

source.place: Theorem 3.3.4, Corollary 3.3.6(1), and Proposition 3.3.8, printed pp.98--102; the centre as adjoint-action kernel over arbitrary non-empty bases. Read online; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Put $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ and $K=\ker(\operatorname{Ad}_G)$. The adjoint-kernel calculus gives the representation, its affine finitely presented closed normal kernel, and their arbitrary base-change compatibility. The relative-centre theorem gives an affine flat finitely presented closed subgroup $Z=Z(G)$, also compatible with arbitrary base change. If $z\in Z(B)$, its image commutes with every dual-number point of $G$ after every $B$-algebra extension, so its conjugation on the tangent module is the identity. Thus $Z\subseteq K$ as subgroup functors, giving a closed immersion $i:Z\hookrightarrow K$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, first two sentences, printed p.102; Theorem 3.3.4, pp.98--100

proof.text: First prove that $i$ is an isomorphism when the base is an algebraically closed field $k$. Write $N=K$ over this field, and let $H=N^0$ have its full open-subscheme structure. The identity-component theorem makes $H$ connected affine of finite type and open and closed in $N$; hence $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(N)$, since tangent vectors at the identity are unchanged on an open neighborhood. The normal-subgroup criterion makes $H$ normal in $G$. The adjoint-kernel calculus identifies this tangent space with $\ker(\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak g})$, which is stable under conjugation by the given maximal torus $T_k$. We will show that it has no nonzero root weight.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, identity-component and Lie-kernel reduction, printed p.102

proof.text: For each root $\alpha$, the rank-one reflection theorem supplies the reductive semisimple-rank-one subgroup $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ and its nonzero root line $\mathfrak g_\alpha$. The torus $T_k$ is maximal in $G_\alpha$, because a larger torus there would be larger in $G_k$. Apply the rank-one classification to this pair. In the $\operatorname{SL}_2$ and $\operatorname{GL}_2$ matrix factors, $[E_{12},E_{21}]=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ is nonzero, including in characteristic two. The extra torus factor is central. In the $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ factor use the quotient map from $\operatorname{GL}_2$. The projective-matrix description gives the chart with bottom-right entry normalized to $1$ around the identity, so the differential sends $E_{12}$ to a nonzero tangent vector (its upper-right coordinate is $\epsilon$). Bracket functoriality sends $[E_{12},E_{11}]=-E_{12}$ to its nonzero negative there. The same computations with indices interchanged treat the negative root. In every model each root line therefore contains a vector with nonzero bracket with another vector. Injectivity and bracket compatibility of the subgroup tangent map carry this back to $\mathfrak g$. Thus no root line is contained in $\ker(\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak g})$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, rank-one reduction and final bracket calculations, printed p.102

proof.text: Use the weight decomposition for the $T_k$-representation on $\operatorname{Lie}(N)$ and the root decomposition of $\mathfrak g$. The inclusion is equivariant, so its $m$-weight subspace maps into the $m$-weight subspace of $\mathfrak g$: compare coefficients of the linearly independent monomials in $k[M]$. Every nonzero weight in $\mathfrak g$ is a root, and its space is one-dimensional. A nonzero intersection with such a line would contain the whole line, contrary to step 3. Hence $\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(T_k)$, the zero-weight subspace. The full torus action on $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ is consequently trivial. Torus-action Lie rigidity, applied to the connected possibly nonreduced group $H$, makes conjugation by $T_k$ trivial on $H$. Thus $H\subseteq C_G(T_k)=T_k$ by the field self-centralizer theorem. All these inclusions concern subgroup schemes and all algebra-valued points.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, torus-action rigidity and weight-space argument, printed p.102

proof.text: Since $H$ is a closed subgroup of the split torus $T_k$, the split-torus subgroup theorem makes it diagonalizable of finite type, with no reducedness assumption. Normality supplies the conjugation action $G\times H\to H$ by group automorphisms. The connected-action multiplicative-type rigidity theorem applies because $G$ is smooth connected, so this action is trivial: $H$ is central in $G$. The normal-subgroup centrality criterion now makes $N$ central. Thus $N\subseteq Z(G)$ as subgroup functors, and step 1 gives the reverse inclusion. This proves $i$ is an isomorphism over every algebraically closed field in every characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, central identity component implies central kernel, printed p.102; the multiplicative-type rigidity alternative avoids needing the intersection-of-all-tori clause of Corollary 3.3.6(2)

proof.text: Return to the arbitrary ring $A$. By the centre and adjoint-kernel base-change statements, every geometric fibre of $i$ is the isomorphism just proved. For each residue field $\kappa(s)$, flatness of $i_s$ follows from flatness after the algebraic-closure extension by pointwise flat descent; that extension is faithfully flat, and every point lifts. The geometric fibre equalities also give surjectivity of $i$ on underlying points: for a point of $K$, extend its residue field to an algebraically closed field and lift along the corresponding geometric-fibre isomorphism. Apply the fibrewise flatness criterion to $Z\xrightarrow{i}K\to\operatorname{Spec}A$: its source structure map is flat and locally of finite presentation by step 1, its target structure map is locally of finite type by step 1, and every fibre map is flat. Thus $i$ is flat. A flat surjective closed immersion is an isomorphism. This proves $Z(G)=K$ over $A$, with no Noetherian or reducedness assumption.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8, fibral reduction by Lemma B.3.1, printed p.102; here B.3.1 is expanded using the existing flatness and closed-immersion criteria

proof.text: For each $A$-algebra $B$, the kernel of the restricted conjugation action on $T(B)$ is $T(B)\cap K(B)$ by the definition of a restricted action, hence $T(B)\cap Z(G)(B)$. This identifies the two subgroup functors, not merely geometric points. For an arbitrary $A\to B$, both $K_B$ and $Z(G)_B$ are the corresponding kernel and centre of $G_B$ by their base-change statements. Pulling back their equality and then intersecting with $T_B$ gives the asserted compatibilities under every further extension. If $B$ is the zero ring all represented functors have their unique empty-scheme point, so the equalities still hold. This includes nonreduced and disconnected $B$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.8 and restriction to the maximal torus; Theorem 3.3.4 base-change compatibility, printed pp.98--102

Source check: Conrad's Reductive Group Schemes has no local copy, so I fetched the public PDF and read Thm 3.3.4 proof p.100 (normal subgroup central iff its identity component is central, CGP 5.3.2), Cor 3.3.6 p.101 and Prop 3.3.8 with its full proof p.102. The 7 steps follow Conrad: Z⊆K; Lie(ker Ad)=ker ad; no root line lies in ker ad, via the rank-one classification ([E12,E21]≠0 in sl2/gl2 even in char 2, [E12,E11]≠0 in pgl2 using the PGL2 chart); weights give Lie(N)⊂Lie(T); torus tangent rigidity puts N^0 inside C_G(T)=T. One difference from Conrad: instead of Cor 3.3.6(2) the delivery shows N^0 is diagonalizable and uses rigidity of a smooth connected action on a multiplicative-type group, a valid cited route. Step 6 is a fibral argument; all hypotheses checked (pointwise flat descent, Z flat and lfp, K lft, flat surjective closed immersion is an isomorphism). The three new statement-only nodes are true and not duplicates. The adjoint-kernel calculus node holds since L is dual to finite projective e^*Ω and GL(L) is affine fp; existing nodes are field-only, char-0-only or field-points-only. Torus Lie rigidity (CGP A.8.11) is proved via the T-action on O/m^n plus injectivity of O(H)→Ô for connected H; tested on α_{p^2}. The normal-subgroup neutral test (CGP 5.3.2) is proved via a commutator homomorphism into central N^0 that dies on the derived group and the central torus; tested on μ_p⊂SL_p and Frobenius kernels. None restates an item clause.
